title: CS: Data Structures and Algorithms
description: For intermediate CS learners reviewing data structures, algorithms, correctness, and complexity. Bounds state important assumptions; n is item count, V vertices, E edges, and h tree height unless otherwise specified.

sources.name: Original educational explanations from general subject knowledge

cards.back: A finite, well-defined procedure for solving a problem or computing a result.
A specification of values and supported operations independent of a particular implementation, such as a stack's push and pop.
A concrete organization of data chosen to support operations efficiently.
An asymptotic upper bound: f(n) is O(g(n)) if f(n) is at most a constant multiple of g(n) for all sufficiently large n.
An asymptotic lower bound: f(n) is Omega(g(n)) if it is at least a positive constant multiple of g(n) for sufficiently large n.
A tight asymptotic bound: both an upper and a lower constant-multiple bound hold for sufficiently large input sizes.
The maximum resource use among inputs of a given size. It is distinct from the notation used to bound that function.
Expected resource use over a specified distribution of inputs. The assumed distribution matters.
Cost per operation over a sequence, distributing occasional expensive operations across the sequence without assuming random inputs.

cards.front: Expected complexity of a randomized algorithm
cards.back: Resource use averaged over the algorithm's random choices, possibly for a fixed input; this differs from averaging over input distributions.
Extra working memory beyond the input storage, with conventions about output storage stated separately.
An operation whose asymptotic cost is bounded independently of input size under the chosen computation model, such as fixed-width array indexing.
The cost increases slowly as input grows multiplicatively; repeated halving commonly gives this bound.
The cost is proportional to input size up to constants, as in a complete scan of n elements.
Typical of efficient comparison sorting such as merge sort.
Typical of examining all pairs of n items with constant work per pair.
Typical of enumerating all subsets of n items, ignoring additional per-subset work.
Typical of enumerating all permutations of n distinct items, ignoring additional output-construction work.
Add their costs; two O(n) scans remain O(n), while an O(n) scan followed by O(n squared) work is O(n squared).
Count total iterations. Two independent loops of length n nested together give O(n squared), but not every nested loop has that bound.
Changing between fixed bases greater than one changes only a constant factor, so O(log n) is base-independent.
For numeric problems, input size is often the number of bits, not the numeric value. A loop to value N can be exponential in log N.
An equation expressing an algorithm's cost using costs on smaller inputs plus local work.
T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1), giving O(log n) time under constant-time random access and comparison.
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), giving Theta(n log n) time in the standard implementation.
A property maintained before and after each iteration, useful for proving correctness.
A proof that a process cannot continue forever, often using a nonnegative integer measure that strictly decreases.
A requirement that must hold before an operation for its stated guarantees to apply.
A property guaranteed after a correctly executed operation whose preconditions held.
A sequence stored so positions can be accessed directly by index, commonly in contiguous memory.
O(1) under a random-access model with fixed-size elements or references.
O(n) worst case because the target may be last or absent.
O(n) worst case when later elements must shift to make space.
O(n) worst case if preserving order requires shifting later elements.
An array-backed sequence that reallocates a larger buffer when capacity is exhausted.
O(1) amortized with geometric capacity growth; a single resizing append can cost O(n).
Length is the number of stored items; capacity is the number that fit in the allocated buffer before resizing.
Multiplying capacity by a constant greater than one yields a geometric series of copying costs and O(1) amortized append.
Adjacent elements often share cache lines, making sequential scans efficient in practice.
Nodes contain a value and a reference to the next node.
Nodes reference both previous and next nodes, supporting bidirectional traversal.
O(n) in the worst case because nodes must be followed rather than directly indexed.
O(1) when a new node is linked before the current head.

cards.front: Singly linked-list deletion after a known node
cards.back: O(1) pointer updates when the predecessor and target are known; finding them may take O(n).

cards.front: Doubly linked-list deletion of a known node
cards.back: O(1) link updates when the node and needed endpoint bookkeeping are available.
O(1) if a tail reference is maintained; otherwise locating the tail can require O(n).
A dummy node used to simplify boundary cases such as insertion or deletion at an endpoint.
A list whose final next link returns to the first node rather than a null endpoint.
A last-in, first-out abstract data type supporting push and pop.
Managing nested function calls, undo histories, expression evaluation, or depth-first search.
O(1) for linked implementations; O(1) amortized for ordinary dynamic-array implementations.
A first-in, first-out abstract data type supporting enqueue and dequeue.
Breadth-first search, task scheduling, or processing arrivals in order.
Maintaining head and tail references supports O(1) enqueue and dequeue.
A fixed-capacity array whose logical positions wrap around, useful for queues and streams.
A double-ended queue supporting insertion and removal at both ends, often in O(1) time.
An abstract data type returning an item of highest or lowest priority rather than earliest arrival.
A complete binary tree usually stored in an array, satisfying a parent-child heap-order condition.
Each parent's key is no greater than its children's keys, making the root a minimum.
Each parent's key is no smaller than its children's keys, making the root a maximum.
With zero-based array indexing, a node at i has children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 when those indexes exist.
For zero-based index i greater than zero, the parent is at floor((i - 1) / 2).
O(1) for a min-heap because the minimum is stored at the root.
O(log n) worst case, appending and moving the new item upward as needed.
O(log n) worst case, replacing the root with the last item and restoring heap order downward.
Builds a heap from an unsorted array in O(n), not O(n log n), by sifting internal nodes downward.
O(n) worst case because heap order does not fully order siblings or subtrees.
A structure mapping keys to storage locations using a hash function and a collision-resolution scheme.
Two distinct keys map to the same hash or bucket; correct implementations resolve this without confusing key identity.
Expected O(1) under suitable hashing and controlled load, but O(n) worst case for common implementations without stronger guarantees.
The ratio of stored entries to available buckets or slots; high load can increase collision costs.
A collision strategy storing multiple entries in a bucket, often in a linked list or another local structure.
A collision strategy storing all entries in the table and probing other slots when a collision occurs.
Open addressing that checks successive slots, wrapping around; it can create primary clustering.
A deletion marker that preserves probe chains so lookups do not stop too early.
Allocating a new table and relocating entries, typically O(n) for that resize and amortized over updates.
Equal keys must have equal hashes; key hash and equality behavior must remain compatible while stored.
A hash map associates keys with values; a hash set tracks membership of keys alone.
A connected acyclic undirected graph, or a rooted hierarchical structure derived from one.
A finite tree with n vertices has n - 1 edges.
A node with no children.
The number of edges from the root to a node, taking root depth as zero.
The maximum root-to-leaf edge count under the edge-count convention; a one-node tree has height zero.
A rooted tree where each node has at most two children, usually distinguished as left and right.
A binary tree in which every node has either zero or two children.
A binary tree with all levels full except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right.
A binary tree in which every internal node has two children and all leaves have the same depth.
Keys in the left subtree are smaller and keys in the right are larger under a chosen ordering; duplicate policies must be defined separately.
Search, insertion, and deletion take O(h), where h is tree height; h may be O(n) in an unbalanced tree.
A search tree maintaining structural bounds that keep height O(log n), supporting efficient ordered operations.
A binary search tree maintaining a height difference of at most one between a node's left and right subtrees.
A balanced search tree using node colors and structural invariants to keep height O(log n).
A local restructuring that changes parent-child links while preserving binary search tree in-order order.
Visit the left subtree, the node, then the right subtree; on a binary search tree this yields keys in sorted order.
Visit the node before its child subtrees; useful for serializing a tree with structure markers.
Visit child subtrees before the node; useful for computing values from children or deleting an entire tree.
Visit nodes by increasing depth, usually with a queue; it is breadth-first traversal.
O(n) time to visit all n nodes; auxiliary space depends on traversal strategy and tree shape.
A prefix tree storing sequences by shared prefixes, useful for dictionaries and autocomplete.
O(L) for a key of length L when each child transition is O(1); memory and alphabet representation affect practical cost.
A balanced multiway search tree with multiple keys per node, designed to reduce external-memory accesses.
A multiway index storing records or record pointers at leaves, often with linked leaves for efficient range scans.
A set of vertices and edges representing relationships.
A graph whose edges have a direction from one vertex to another.
A graph whose edges connect endpoints without an orientation.
A graph whose edges carry values such as distances, costs, or capacities.
A graph with no self-loops and no parallel edges, under the usual convention.

cards.front: Vertex degree in an undirected graph
cards.back: The number of incident edge ends; a self-loop contributes two when loops are allowed.
In a directed graph, in-degree counts incoming edges and out-degree counts outgoing edges.
A path follows successive edges; a cycle returns to its starting vertex without repeating intermediate vertices in a simple cycle.
A maximal set of vertices mutually reachable in an undirected graph.
A maximal set of directed-graph vertices where every vertex can reach every other.
A directed graph with no directed cycles, useful for dependencies and prerequisites.
A representation storing each vertex's neighbors; space is O(V + E), with undirected edges typically listed twice.
A V by V table of edges or weights, using O(V squared) space and O(1) edge-existence lookup.
A graph with relatively few edges compared with the possible V squared scale; adjacency lists are commonly suitable.
Explores a graph in layers using a queue; it finds shortest path lengths in an unweighted graph.
O(V + E) time for a full traversal and O(V) auxiliary memory for standard visited, queue, and predecessor storage.
Explores a branch deeply before backtracking, using recursion or an explicit stack.
O(V + E) for a full traversal, with O(V) auxiliary space in the standard implementation.
To avoid repeated exploration and infinite cycling, and to keep graph traversals within their intended bounds.
An ordering of a directed graph's vertices in which every edge goes from earlier to later; it exists exactly when the graph is acyclic.
Repeatedly remove an in-degree-zero vertex and update its neighbors; failure to output all vertices indicates a directed cycle.
O(V + E) using adjacency lists and a queue of zero-in-degree vertices, or a suitable DFS implementation.
Computes single-source shortest paths in a graph with nonnegative edge weights by repeatedly settling the smallest tentative distance.
A standard adjacency-list implementation runs in O((V + E) log V), with implementation-dependent handling of priority updates.
A later negative edge can improve a distance already treated as final, invalidating the greedy settling argument.
Relaxes all edges repeatedly to find single-source shortest paths with negative edges and detect reachable negative-weight cycles; standard time is O(VE).
A dynamic-programming all-pairs shortest-path method taking O(V cubed) time and O(V squared) space; finite shortest paths require no relevant negative cycles.
A minimum-total-weight set of edges connecting all vertices of a connected undirected weighted graph without cycles.
A collection of trees spanning the components of a disconnected undirected graph.
Sort edges by weight and add each edge that joins separate components, usually using disjoint sets to detect cycles.
O(E log E) for comparison sorting plus near-linear disjoint-set work in a standard implementation.
Grows a minimum spanning tree by repeatedly adding the least-weight edge connecting the current tree to an outside vertex.

cards.front: Prim with adjacency lists and a binary heap
cards.back: Runs in O((V + E) log V), commonly stated as O(E log V) for connected graphs with at least two vertices.
A structure maintaining a partition into disjoint sets, supporting find and union operations.
During a disjoint-set find, redirect visited nodes toward the root to accelerate future operations.
Attach the smaller or lower-rank disjoint-set tree below the larger one to limit tree growth.
Path compression combined with union by rank or size gives O(alpha(n)) amortized time per operation, where inverse Ackermann grows extremely slowly.
Scan items until finding the target or reaching the end; O(n) worst-case time and O(1) auxiliary space for a simple iterative scan.
The search domain must have a monotone ordering or predicate; the usual array version requires sorted data and efficient random access.
Maintain a clear interval convention, such as [lo, hi), and consistently exclude positions proved impossible to avoid off-by-one errors.
A sort preserving the relative order of items with equal keys.
An algorithm using little extra storage beyond its input, often O(1) auxiliary array storage; recursion-stack conventions should be stated.
Sort halves recursively and merge them; standard array merge sort takes O(n log n) time, O(n) extra array storage, and can be stable.
Partition around a pivot and recursively sort partitions; randomized quicksort has expected O(n log n) time and O(n squared) worst-case time.
Build a heap and repeatedly extract its extremum; standard array heapsort takes O(n log n) worst-case time and O(1) auxiliary storage but is not stable.
Build a sorted prefix by inserting each new element; O(n squared) worst case and O(n) best case for already sorted data in the usual implementation.
Repeatedly choose the smallest remaining item; O(n squared) comparisons even on sorted input, O(1) auxiliary storage, and usually unstable.
Repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order items; O(n squared) worst case, stable with strict comparisons, and O(n) best case with an early-exit check.
Sort integer keys in a bounded range using counts; O(n + k) time for n items and range size k, useful when k is not too large.
Sort by successive digits using a suitable stable digit sort; commonly O(d(n + b)) for d digits and base b.
Any general comparison sort requires Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case for n distinct items.
A partition-based selection algorithm finding a kth order statistic in expected O(n) time with random pivots, but O(n squared) worst case without stronger pivot rules.
Solve smaller subproblems recursively and combine their results, as in merge sort.
Make a locally best choice at each step; correctness requires a problem-specific justification, not merely intuition.
Reuse solutions to overlapping subproblems with suitable optimal substructure or recurrence relationships.
Top-down caching of computed subproblem results, usually alongside recursion.
Bottom-up dynamic programming that fills a table in an order satisfying dependencies.
Explore choices recursively, undoing decisions when a partial solution cannot or should not continue.
Maintain information about a moving contiguous interval, often giving linear time when each endpoint moves only forward.
Use coordinated indexes to exploit order or structure, such as finding a pair sum in a sorted array in O(n).
Store cumulative totals so a static range sum can be answered in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.
A Fenwick tree supports point updates and prefix-sum queries in O(log n) with O(n) storage.
A hierarchical interval structure commonly supporting point updates and range aggregate queries in O(log n) with O(n) storage.
A stack maintained in sorted order, useful for next-greater-element problems; each item is typically pushed and popped at most once.

cards.front: Cycle detection in a linked list
cards.back: Floyd's slow-and-fast-pointer method detects a cycle in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
Maintain a size-k heap while scanning n items, giving O(n log k) time for k at least two and O(k) extra storage.
Compare the pattern at each possible text position; worst-case time is O(nm) for text length n and pattern length m.
Uses a prefix or failure table to avoid rechecking text, achieving O(n + m) time and O(m) auxiliary storage.
BFS minimizes edge count in an unweighted graph; Dijkstra minimizes total weight when weights are nonnegative.

cards.front: Minimum spanning tree versus shortest-path tree
cards.back: An MST minimizes total connecting-edge weight; a shortest-path tree minimizes source-to-vertex distances. They need not coincide.
P contains decision problems solvable in polynomial time; NP contains decision problems whose yes certificates are verifiable in polynomial time. Whether P equals NP is unresolved.
A decision problem in NP to which every NP problem can be reduced in polynomial time; a polynomial-time algorithm for one would imply P equals NP.
A problem at least as hard as every NP problem under the chosen polynomial reduction; it need not itself be in NP or even be a decision problem.
